query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin titanium interlayer within HEA multilayers will promote a transition from diffusion‐mediated to dislocation‐mediated creep by enhancing interface coherency.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers deposited without a dedicated transition layer, exhibiting less coherent interfaces that favor diffusion‐mediated creep mechanisms at lower stresses and intermediate temperatures.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin titanium interlayer between the HEA layers using magnetron sputtering, systematically varying its thickness and composition.
generation.conditions: Samples should be prepared under controlled deposition conditions and subsequently tested via nanoindentation or micro-compression creep experiments across a temperature and stress regime covering both diffusion and dislocation creep regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The titanium interlayer, due to its intermediate lattice parameter, is expected to improve interface coherency between adjacent HEA layers.
generation.mechanism: Titanium’s lattice parameter bridges the mismatch between HEA layers, reducing the driving force for rapid atomic diffusion at the interface while still allowing dislocation motion under applied stress. This improved coherency is expected to suppress diffusion-mediated creep and promote dislocation-based mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: The presence of the titanium interlayer should yield a measurable shift in creep behavior, with a decrease in diffusion-dominated creep rates and an increased prominence of dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, observable as a changing stress exponent and a higher yield strength in creep tests.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers fabricated without an interlayer, where diffusion-mediated creep is predominantly observed under the same testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The anticipated effect is expected within a moderate temperature and stress window where interface coherency is a dominant factor; at very high temperatures or extreme stresses, other mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary sliding or void formation) may override the interlayer's influence.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and compositional tuning of the titanium interlayer necessary to achieve the desired level of coherency is uncertain and may require further refinement. Additionally, interactions with the intrinsic properties of the HEA layers under varying thermal conditions add uncertainty to the magnitude of the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer films using magnetron sputtering: one set incorporating a thin titanium interlayer (with various controlled thicknesses) and one set without any interlayer. Subject both sets to identical creep testing conditions (using nanoindentation or micro-compression) across a temperature and stress range that covers both creep regimes. Characterize the interface structure using TEM and measure lattice parameters via XRD.
measurements: Interface coherency and lattice mismatch metrics
Dislocation activity and morphology via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA multilayers with the titanium interlayer do not show a statistically significant shift from diffusion-mediated creep (baseline behavior) toward dislocation-mediated creep (e.g., altered stress exponent, dislocation patterns) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. As a result, precipitation strengthening should be considered in developing HEAs for high temperature applications. chosen.lever: interlayer composition to modulate interface coherency
chosen.technique: magnetron sputtering deposition of HEA multilayers with a deliberately engineered transition interlayer followed by standardized creep tests
chosen.conditions: Depositions performed under reproducible conditions with systematic variation of interlayer composition and testing across a temperature and stress range that brackets the transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep
chosen.why: This experimental approach directly inverts the niche by actively controlling the degree of interface coherency via the interlayer material. By selecting a transition material that offers intermediate lattice matching between adjacent HEA layers, the study isolates its effect on the creep mechanism. Routine thin-film deposition and creep characterization techniques in the field make this a plausible and rigorous strategy to resolve the open question.
